title: Nine Years In, iOS Is Slowing Down. How Did the Operating System of the Mobile Era Shape Our Lives?
excerpt: From iPhone OS 1.0 in 2007 to this year's iOS 9, how has this mobile operating system changed our lives?
body:
From iPhone OS 1.0 in 2007 to this year's iOS 9, how has this mobile operating system changed our lives?

This is the ninth year of iOS, Apple's mobile operating system. At this year's Worldwide Developers Conference (WWDC), Apple announced the ninth version. Unlike the big overhauls of past years, [iOS 9 is little more than an "interior renovation"](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/10562.html): longer battery life, more storage, a slightly smarter Siri and Apple Maps, a new Home app for controlling smart-home products, and a new News app.

After nine years, iOS has matured so far that it is hard to imagine how it grew out of the bare-bones iPhone OS of 2007. Step by step, how has each year's update changed and shaped our lives?

## iPhone OS 1.0: The iPhone Is Born

![The original iPhone running iPhone OS 1.0](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201606071737003UFqArwO9a7HzbfW.jpg-w600)

Image: [wired.co.uk](http://www.wired.co.uk/news/archive/2013-06/12/ios-evolution/viewgallery/304957)

- "A breakthrough five years ahead of the industry." That is how Steve Jobs described the first iPhone at its launch. Apple had wanted to bring all of Mac OS X to the iPhone, but only Mobile Safari made it onto the phone, short of what was expected. The iPhone was pitched as an iPod that could make calls and go online, and those were the main features Jobs showed on stage: a browser, an iPod and a phone.
- With its cleaner industrial design, the iPhone dropped the physical keyboard and gained a larger screen. Many other phone makers, chasing differentiation, were turning out oddly shaped handsets, such as the slider Nokia N81.
- To draw users in with good services that already existed, Apple partnered with Google. The built-in services included search, maps and YouTube.

These features look far too simple today, but that did not stop the iPhone from changing history. In the early 2000s, Microsoft, Palm and other smartphone makers had tried to push full-touchscreen phones. The touch experience was so poor, though, that from 2005 on the industry went back almost entirely to phones with full QWERTY keyboards.

Apple did not invent the virtual keyboard, but with a capacitive touchscreen and multi-touch it replaced the physical one. That shift showed that consuming content now mattered more than text communication such as email and text messages, and it carried the smartphone from a business tool to the mass market.

GPS and maps also became standard on smartphones. On March 6, 2008, Apple formally named its first mobile operating system iPhone OS, and the iPod touch began running it too.

## iPhone OS 2.0: The App Store Arrives

![The iPhone 3G](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607173700NUQ0uzIv7LCwjq62.jpg-w600)

Image: [feelgrafix](http://feelgrafix.com/959085-iphone-3g.html)

- When iPhone OS 2.0 arrived in 2008, the iPhone finally got 3G. The App Store went live three months after Apple released the beta SDK. That October, Google followed with the Android Market, which later became the Google Play Store.

At first the store offered only small games and simple tools, but it is no exaggeration to call the app store the most important change of the past decade.

In its heyday, Microsoft, as a software company, made acquisition after acquisition and used its platform advantage in ways that mostly hurt developers. Apple turned software development into a business. As the iPhone sold better and better, the App Store drew in large numbers of developers. It was also relatively friendly to them: the iPhone Human Interface Guidelines and the design elements built into the development kit made it much easier to build a good app.

What kept developers in the end was the money. Apple split revenue 70/30 in developers' favor, whereas traditional software retail channels often took half, and in the early days of China's phone distribution channels developers got as little as 20%. According to figures from WWDC 2015, App Store apps have now been downloaded more than 100 billion times and have earned developers more than US$30 billion. More and more developers have joined in.

An app with enough downloads could make its developers wealthy in a short time. Beyond companies that made money by selling software directly, social-networking startups also found it easier to get going in the mobile era.

With hardware and software growing together, Apple smoothly shaped users' habits. Seven years on, the average user has 119 apps, and apps are downloaded 850 times every second.

## iPhone OS 3.0: A New Way to Pay for Apps

![iPhone OS 3.0](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607173701tSkKPvgXmIiUZyDE.jpg-w600)

Image: [wired.co.uk](http://www.wired.co.uk/news/archive/2013-06/12/ios-evolution#viewgallery/305103)

- To match the multitasking of its rival Android, iPhone OS 3.0 introduced push notifications and Spotlight, a system-wide search, to give a similar feel. Apple also opened more interfaces to third-party developers.
- By 2009 Apple was selling more iPhones and was content to make its money from hardware. Meanwhile, in-app purchase (IAP) in the App Store began to spur users to spend.

The changes to the user experience, and the disruption of the industry, went on. Push notifications let alerts from apps running in the background come straight to you; before, only email could do that. These notifications need your permission. They also changed how users get information.

Many apps in the store are still labeled "in-app purchase." Free or paid, an app that lets users spend some time absorbed in it makes them more willing to pay. Many apps offer a pro version. The effect is most obvious in mobile games. You pay for the game, and once you reach a certain level, you often go on to buy character gear or new dungeons to level up or keep playing. This even gave rise to a huge mobile-gaming industry. By 2014, global mobile-game revenue had reached US$25 billion.

## iOS 4.0: The Retina Display and the iPad

![The iPhone 4](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607173701SjNhdzuf1mMgQAbV.jpg-w600)

Image: [awoltrends](http://awoltrends.com/2012/04/rationalism/)

- With the fourth generation, iPhone OS was renamed to the name you know better: iOS. In 2010 iPhone sales nearly doubled from the year before, and rapid growth had begun. The iPhone 4's industrial design left every competitor behind. As late as 2014, Chinese phone makers such as Xiaomi and Smartisan were still touting glass on front and back as a design highlight.
- When news of the Retina display leaked, many people doubted it. But the iPhone 4 did raise pixel density by about 50%. After it came out, competitors' phones were still using 800 x 480 resolution.
- In the iOS 4 era Apple's wider ecosystem was still being built, and its hardware did better than its software. FaceTime, the native video-chat app, appeared on the home screen, and to promote it Apple kept out other third-party apps of the same kind.
- Android-style multitasking finally arrived. The difference was that, to save memory, iOS 4 let apps sit in the background without running code that would compete for resources.
- iAd, a better-designed and more polished ad service, launched to no response.

When you buy a phone today, you check the screen's pixels. Users learned to care about this gradually, after the Retina-class screen appeared with iOS 4. Despite a fourfold jump in resolution, the system kept old apps working properly. As users went from accepting sharp displays to demanding them, the Retina screen became the standard. We can no longer see pixels, even on a 2,000-yuan Chinese phone.

Once the system had matured, Apple turned back to hardware, this time the iPad. iPad sales have fallen over the past two years, but in 2010 the iPad made the tablet a new category of consumer electronics. Microsoft had long tried to bring its own tablets to the mass market, but they ended up as professional devices for businesses, still trailing a stylus.

## iOS 5.0: Mobile Replaces Desktop, and the iPhone Breaks Free of the Computer

![The iPhone 4s](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607173701fIuMBNyGecJ4qPA3.jpg-w600)

Image: [The Verge](http://www.theverge.com/apple/2011/10/12/2484524/iphone-4s-review)

- The iPhone now brought in most of Apple's cash flow. It had to become an ecosystem of its own; the image of a Mac accessory no longer fit. Starting with the iPhone 4s, Apple's mobile devices no longer had to connect to iTunes the first time they were switched on, or to update their system through iTunes. They could update the system and apps over the internet, on the device itself.
- For an Apple that wanted to own everything and loosen carriers' control, iMessage came a little late. Still, it hit the existing text-messaging business, though in China you are more likely to use WeChat.
- Siri, the AI voice assistant, may get more use as something to tease. It can do only a limited number of things and often fails to understand what you say.
- iBooks, which took on Kindle for share of the publishing market, did not succeed. Apple also built Newsstand for traditional newspapers and magazines, and that failed too. Today, though, news content adapts itself to apps, rather than each app getting its own custom format suited to the content.

Once people no longer needed a PC to register and update their phones, they came to rely on the iPhone more and more. iCloud, launched with iOS 5.0, also improved storage and the protection of private data. Within a self-contained iPhone ecosystem, iCloud began to make sense only when users gathered their photos, contact backups and other information in it. MobileMe, a similar service from the iPhone OS 2.0 era, had been little more than a backup.

Siri looked promising, but Apple did not make it a headline service. You have to press and hold the Home button to summon it, and nothing on screen tells you so. Still, it has been slowly gathering data and getting smarter. Proactive in iOS 9 looks like progress.

## iOS 6.0: Laying the Groundwork for Payments, as Phones Enter Everyday Spending

![The iPhone 5](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607173702XYZUrfjVu6qOKdlB.jpg-w600)

Image: [wired](http://www.wired.com/2012/09/iphone5-lte-model/)

- Over the previous few versions, Apple had added a lot of digital content to the iPhone, including articles and TV. For a better viewing experience, the iPhone 5 got a bigger screen.
- After a long period of competition and negotiation, Apple dropped Google Maps and preinstalled its own maps app.
- A brand-new app, Passbook, could hold boarding passes, membership cards and movie tickets. It also supported store coupons and stored-value cards, and once Apple opened it to third parties, passes and cards could update in real time. It looked like the forerunner of a digital wallet.

Android used the advantages of open source to attract developers and users quickly. By 2012 it had become a far bigger platform than iOS: according to IDC, Android held 68.1% of the smartphone market. Google's business model, making money not from hardware but from services and advertising, threatened Apple.

Until the iPhone 6 gained an NFC chip, Passbook relied mainly on QR codes for payment, which had problems with both security and convenience. This native Apple app also supported few third parties, and even fewer in China. An app that sounded convenient never won over most users. Even so, it created new uses for the smartphone, such as boarding flights and buying movie tickets. Passbook also got users into the habit of paying by phone, laying the groundwork for Apple's later push of Apple Pay.

## iOS 7.0: A New Look, and Getting Users Used to Fingerprints

![iOS 7](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607173702eUCWmKiOqwJZPAV4.jpg-w600)

Image: appadvice

- iOS 7 was the biggest visual overhaul since the system first launched. Apple moved from skeuomorphism to a flat design language. From then on, apps on the iPhone no longer looked like raised buttons but like doors set flush into the screen, while a frosted-glass blur gave the screen a sense of depth.
- Apple's own apps, such as Pages, Numbers, iMovie and Keynote, all became free and began syncing with their Mac versions, so users no longer had to buy them twice.
- With the fingerprint-reading Home button on the iPhone 5s, iOS 7 also began supporting fingerprint recognition, though for now only to unlock the phone.
- AirDrop, which transfers files between devices on the same network and had existed only on the Mac, came to iOS 7 as well. It worked exactly the same way, and two iPhones could now swap files over Bluetooth.
- Control Center also appeared. A swipe up from the bottom of the screen now brings up a menu with one-tap controls for Wi-Fi, volume and other common functions.
- FaceTime, the iPhone's built-in video-calling service, added audio-only calls, so on Wi-Fi users could make calls without paying the carrier's call rates at all.
- iOS 7 can also update all apps with one tap, instead of updating them one by one.

Apple abandoned skeuomorphic design entirely. Under Jony Ive, Apple's chief design officer, iOS 7 ushered in the era of flat design, though the change drew complaints from all sides at first. Judging by how attitudes later shifted, a more direct and efficient design language really was the future. The redesign also forced a huge number of third-party developers to rework their app designs, or even rebuild their apps. Within a few months, users and developers had adapted to the new style, and neither wanted to go back.

Fingerprint recognition did more to change daily life. Thanks to its simple product line, Apple put the Touch ID fingerprint sensor into the hands of tens of millions of users within a few months. At the time, iOS 7 limited fingerprint recognition to Apple's own apps, and the feature served only to train users' habits. Once users got used to fingerprints instead of typing passwords, Apple would have more say. In hindsight, the Touch ID that shipped with iOS 7 also laid the groundwork for today's Apple Pay mobile payments and for fingerprints in place of passwords in third-party apps.

## iOS 8.0: A Complete Mobile Operating System

![iOS 8](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607173703S6tdJ5FhLuWceyHa.jpg-w600)

Image: [mashable](http://mashable.com/2014/06/04/ios-8-features/)

- After Samsung, HTC and other Android makers had all released phones with screens over 5 inches, Apple finally launched the iPhone 6, with 4.7- and 5.5-inch screens, in September 2014. iOS 8, updated at the same time, added features for handling a big screen. For example, lightly double-tapping the Home button slides the screen down so your thumb can reach the top.
- Released alongside iOS 8 was Swift, a new programming language, with which Apple hoped to give developers a faster, easier way to write software for iOS devices.
- The most eye-catching thing in iOS 8 was not the design but HealthKit, which lets anyone take part in medical research with a phone, and HomeKit, which lets smart-home hardware connect. This meant more ordinary people, as well as third-party developers, could join the ecosystem.
- iCloud Drive, an upgraded version of Apple's cloud service, not only backs up your files in the cloud but also syncs them better between an iPhone and a Mac laptop.

Once the iPhone 6 also went big, sales shot up. According to Strategy Analytics, Apple sold 74.5 million iPhones in the fourth quarter of 2014, up 46% year on year. And although OS X and iOS were not merged into one system, iCloud Drive and Handoff, which lets people take phone calls, text messages and video calls on a computer, tied the iPhone and the Mac more closely together.

More important, Apple began opening fingerprint recognition, HomeKit hardware access and other permissions to third-party developers, although over the past year we have not seen any such hardware come out.

The pieces are now in place for the iPhone to replace passwords, and even to become the hub of the devices in the home. iOS 8.0 can be seen as the point at which iOS matured in functionality, with new areas, including smart homes and health services, left for new internet services and even hardware to fill.

It was also after iOS 8.0 launched that Apple formally released the Apple Watch and its operating system, watchOS 1.0. This is Tim Cook's own iPhone, and Apple's biggest challenge since 2007.
